intro:
A phone order form template for restaurants should capture the caller’s name, phone number, items, sizes, modifiers, notes, and pickup time. It should also give your team a simple way to read the order back before it goes to the kitchen.

For a busy pizza shop, deli, takeout counter, or family restaurant, the goal is not fancy. The goal is fewer mistakes, faster calls, and a ticket your kitchen can actually use. Tools like [ROAL](/how-it-works) can help by answering the phone, taking the order from your live menu, and sending a clean ticket to the kitchen screen.

sections.h2: What should a restaurant phone order form capture?
sections.body:
A good template should match the way real phone orders happen in your shop. Keep it short enough to use during a rush, but complete enough that the kitchen does not have to guess.

Use these fields:
- Caller name
- Callback number
- Pickup or delivery
- Order items
- Size or portion
- Modifiers, like extra cheese or no onions
- Special notes
- Quoted ready time
- Staff initials or caller ID note

Here is a simple line your team can use on the phone: "Can I get your name, best number, and the items you'd like today?"

If you want a starter template, think in this order:
1. Who is calling?
2. What are they ordering?
3. What changes do they want?
4. Is this pickup or delivery?
5. What time should they arrive?

sections.h2: How do you lay out the form so staff can use it fast?
sections.body:
The best form is one that follows the call. Put the most important fields at the top, and leave space for handwritten notes or a screen that can be scanned quickly.

A simple layout for a paper or digital form:
| Field | What to capture |
|---|---|
| Caller | Name and phone number |
| Order type | Pickup or delivery |
| Items | Item, size, quantity |
| Modifiers | Toppings, sides, substitutions |
| Notes | Allergies, no-contact note, building instructions |
| Time | Quoted ready time |
| Status | New, preparing, ready |

For example, say a caller orders a large pepperoni pizza, extra cheese, and one Caesar salad. Your form should make it easy to write: "Large pepperoni, extra cheese, Caesar salad, ready in 20 minutes." Then the kitchen sees the same thing without having to decode the call.

If you use [ROAL](/use-cases/pickup-orders), the ticket already follows this kind of structure: items, modifiers, name, phone, and ready time.

sections.h2: What should the phone script say while filling it out?
sections.body:
A form works better when the script matches it. Keep the wording short and direct so staff can move through the call without sounding stiff.

A practical phone script:
- "Thanks for calling. What can I get started for you?"
- "Is this pickup or delivery?"
- "What size would you like?"
- "Any changes to the order?"
- "Can I read that back to make sure I have it right?"

The read-back matters. It catches mistakes before they hit the kitchen. A simple line works well: "Just to confirm, that’s one large plain pie, one chicken parm hero, no onions, and a ready time of 20 minutes."

If a customer asks something odd, the form should also leave room for staff notes. For example: "Customer asks about parking" or "Allergy question sent to manager." That keeps the call moving without losing the issue.

sections.h2: How do you handle sold-out items, allergies, and tricky calls?
sections.body:
Your template should have a clear place for exceptions. That keeps staff from promising something the kitchen cannot make or answering something sensitive without help.

Use a small checklist on the form:
- Item sold out?
- Allergy question?
- Manager needed?
- Catering request?
- Complaint or refund issue?

A good phone line for sold-out items is: "I’m sorry, we’re out of that today. I can suggest a similar option." For allergy-sensitive questions, the better line is: "Let me get that to a manager so we can be careful with that order."

sections.h2: Should you use paper, a spreadsheet, or an AI phone host?
sections.body:
The right setup depends on how many calls you take and how busy the front counter gets. Paper can work for a very small shop, but it gets messy fast during a rush. A spreadsheet is easier to read later, but staff still have to type while the phone rings.

A quick way to compare:
| Option | Best for | Weak spot |
|---|---|---|
| Paper form | Very small volume | Hard to keep organized |
| Spreadsheet | Simple tracking | Slow during busy hours |
| AI phone host | Busy phone order flows | Tricky calls still need staff |

sections.h2: How should you quote time and confirm the order back?
sections.body:
Pickup time is part of the form, not just part of the conversation. If staff quote too fast, the kitchen gets slammed. If they quote too loosely, callers lose confidence.

Use a consistent method:
1. Check the kitchen load.
2. Pick a realistic ready time.
3. Say it out loud.
4. Write it on the form.
5. Read the full order back.

Example script: "That will be ready in about 25 minutes. Let me read it back to you." Then confirm the items, changes, name, and number.

If you want a number example, say your average phone order is $28. Plug in your own average. If you take 10 phone orders in a shift, that is $280 in order value before any add-ons. A cleaner form helps protect that revenue by reducing remake mistakes and callback confusion. ROAL also quotes a ready time on the call and confirms the order before it sends the ticket.

faq.q: What fields should be on a restaurant phone order form?
faq.a: At minimum, include the caller’s name, phone number, pickup or delivery choice, ordered items, sizes, modifiers, special notes, and the quoted ready time. It also helps to add a spot for sold-out items, allergy questions, and staff initials. That keeps the order clear for both the cashier and the kitchen.

faq.q: How do you take phone orders accurately at a restaurant?
faq.a: Use a repeatable script, ask one question at a time, and read the full order back before hanging up. Write down or capture the item name, size, changes, and any special instructions. A clear read-back is one of the easiest ways to catch mistakes before the order reaches the kitchen.

faq.a: Yes. ROAL can answer the phone, take pickup and delivery orders from the restaurant’s live menu, quote a ready time, confirm the order, and send a clean ticket to the kitchen screen. It also handles common questions and passes tricky calls to staff with a summary.

faq.q: How do I forward my restaurant phone to another number?
faq.a: On many landlines and some carriers, you can dial *72 and then the forwarding number to forward all calls, and *73 to turn it off. On some mobile carriers, codes can differ, and business VoIP systems usually use a web portal. Always confirm the exact code with your carrier or phone system and test with a call.
